Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
You can never know who will harm you

vignette: Maria, a 59-year-old project manager of Mexican heritage, remembers the night her apartment was seized by unknown men. For three weeks she was locked in a small concrete cell, with no windows, no light, and only the dull hum of a ventilation system. The heavy door felt like a coffin's lid, and each breath was a reminder that she was sealed inside a world of fear. When she returns to her office, the sight of a locked conference room door or a meeting that suddenly gets postponed pulls her back to that confinement. A phantom tightness in her neck-just as the cell's walls had constricted her-spreads a wave of alertness. Her home, once a sanctuary, now feels like a prison, and she remains perpetually on guard, even when the front door is unlocked. Those reminders also stir a deeper sadness. Each closing door evokes a memory of being trapped and conjures the image of a life that is no longer happy. She tells herself, "I used to laugh, but now I am always miserable," and this belief deepens an emotional numbness that dampens the joy of everyday moments. Because she is convinced that danger can arise at any moment-"you can never know who will harm you"-she stays hypervigilant. Even while alone in her kitchen, she cannot relax; she is constantly scanning for imagined threats. That persistent fear of harm keeps her from resting, magnifying her feelings of emptiness and despair. Her sense of lost happiness transforms ordinary choices into perceived traps. The lack of options she felt in captivity now colors her perception of the office hierarchy; she sees each decision as a potential lock, a chance to be trapped again. This view reinforces the triggers, turning normal rooms and meetings into painful reminders of her confinement. When the alarm of danger rises, Maria seeks mental strategies that feel like safety nets. She tells herself, "It didn't really happen," hoping to erase the pain. Yet she also ruminates on what she might have done differently, blaming herself for not escaping sooner. To regain a sense of control, she over-analyzes every detail of the event, hoping that understanding will shield her from future harm. Her heightened sense of threat means that even a standard lock-such as the door to the executive breakroom-triggers the same tightness in her neck and surge of anxiety, as if she were back in the cell. This reaction only strengthens her fear of confined spaces and the feeling that she has no options. The self-blame rumination deepens her emotional numbness, leaving her feeling dead inside, while her obsessive over-analysis creates false alarms that keep her in a state of constant vigilance. The magical thinking that the event was not real only reinforces her belief that harm could return, sustaining the cycle of fear and avoidance. After months of missing deadlines and sensing her team's patience erode, Maria finally sought therapy. She fears that her career will crumble if she cannot regain control, yet she also hopes to breathe again, to feel joy, and to believe that the life she once loved can return.
